finding.title: Preserve the empty-input contract
finding.explanation: The removed conditional changes `first([])` from returning `None` to raising `IndexError`. The prior implementation is direct source evidence that empty inputs were intentionally handled; no supplied caller or API change establishes that exceptions are now expected.
finding.user_impact: Any caller passing an empty list or other empty indexable collection can now fail instead of receiving the documented-by-behavior sentinel value.

evidence_items.output_snippet: `first` is called with an empty indexable collection, such as `[]`.

assumptions: The previous `None` result for empty inputs is part of the function's expected behavior because the supplied diff shows an explicit guard.
No evidence was supplied that all callers guarantee non-empty inputs or expect `IndexError`.
limitations: Only the supplied diff was reviewed; callers, tests, and public API documentation were not provided.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore the guard: `return items[0] if items else None`, or explicitly migrate and validate all affected callers if raising on empty input is an intentional API break.

finding.title: Preserve the empty-array result
finding.explanation: The previous implementation explicitly returned `0` when `items.length` was zero. The changed expression evaluates `0 / 0` for an empty array, producing `NaN`. This is a concrete API behavior regression for a supported input shape.
finding.user_impact: Callers passing `[]` now receive `NaN` instead of `0`, which can propagate through later calculations or serialization.

primary_location.snippet: export function average(items: number[]): number { return items.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0) / items.length; }

assumptions: The prior return value of `0` for an empty array is part of the intended behavior; the supplied diff contains no evidence of an intentional contract change.
limitations: Only the supplied one-line diff was available, so affected callers and tests could not be inspected.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore the length guard, for example `return items.length ? items.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / items.length : 0;`, unless the API is intentionally being changed to reject empty arrays; in that case, throw an explicit documented error and update affected callers.

finding.title: Return the sorted collection instead of `None`
finding.explanation: `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`, whereas the previous `sorted(items)` expression returned a new sorted list. The function therefore no longer fulfills its apparent return-value contract and also unexpectedly mutates list inputs.
finding.user_impact: Callers that iterate over, index, or otherwise use the function result will receive `None` and can fail with errors such as `TypeError`. Callers retaining the input list will also observe it reordered.

evidence_items.output_snippet: Any caller passes a list and uses the returned value; mutation is additionally observable whenever the caller retains the original list.

assumptions: The prior implementation defines the intended behavior because no caller or API documentation was supplied.
limitations: The supplied diff does not show affected callers or tests.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore `return sorted(items)` to preserve both the returned-list contract and non-mutating behavior.

finding.title: Preserve support for non-list iterables
finding.explanation: The built-in `sorted()` accepts arbitrary iterables, while `.sort()` is only available on mutable sequence types that implement that method. This narrows the accepted input contract without any guard or conversion.
finding.user_impact: Inputs that previously worked, such as tuples, generators, sets, or dictionary views, now raise `AttributeError` instead of producing a sorted list.

evidence_items.output_snippet: `sorted_items` receives any iterable without a callable `.sort()` method.

assumptions: The broad iterable support of the previous implementation was part of the function's observable contract.
limitations: No type annotations, documentation, or callers were supplied to establish whether inputs are intentionally restricted to lists.
finding.proposed_remedy: Use `return sorted(items)`; if list-only input is intentional, validate and document that contract while still returning the sorted result explicitly.

finding.title: Await the fetcher before reading the response
finding.explanation: The changed code assigns the fetcher's return value directly to `response`. When `fetcher` follows the usual asynchronous fetch contract and returns a Promise, `response.json` is undefined and the function rejects with a `TypeError`. Previously, `await fetcher()` supported both Promise-returning and synchronous fetchers.
finding.user_impact: Calls using an async fetcher can no longer load JSON and fail before processing the response body.

primary_location.snippet: export async function load(fetcher) { const response = fetcher(); return response.json(); }

evidence_items.output_snippet: Invoke `load` with a fetcher that returns a Promise resolving to a response object, such as the standard `fetch` API.

assumptions: `fetcher` may return a Promise, as supported by the previous implementation and implied by the async loading flow.
limitations: No caller or test context was supplied, so the exact fetcher implementations cannot be confirmed.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore `const response = await fetcher();` before calling `response.json()`.

finding.title: False-like strings now evaluate as enabled
finding.explanation: The previous implementation explicitly recognized only case-insensitive `"true"` and `"1"`. Python considers every non-empty string truthy, so the replacement changes `"false"`, `"0"`, and arbitrary text from disabled to enabled.
finding.user_impact: Configurations or inputs using values such as `"false"` or `"0"` can unexpectedly activate the guarded feature or behavior.

evidence_items.output_snippet: `enabled` receives any non-empty string other than a previously accepted true value, including `"false"`, `"0"`, or `"no"`.

assumptions: The function continues to receive string values representing booleans.
The prior accepted-value set defines the intended API contract.
limitations: Only the supplied diff is available; affected callers and tests were not provided.
finding.proposed_remedy: Preserve explicit string parsing, for example `return value.lower() in {'true', '1'}`. If non-string values must also be supported, branch by type and define their accepted semantics explicitly.

finding.title: Pagination uses `size` as an absolute end index
finding.explanation: `Array.prototype.slice(start, end)` interprets its second argument as an exclusive index, not a result length. Replacing `start + size` with `size` therefore changes the API from returning up to `size` items beginning at `start` to returning only indices from `start` through `size - 1`. Existing guards are not visible in the supplied diff; even valid non-negative pagination inputs are affected.
finding.user_impact: For any page with `start > 0`, the function returns too few items; when `start >= size`, it returns an empty array. For example, `page(items, 10, 10)` now returns no items instead of indices 10–19.

primary_location.snippet: export function page(items, start, size) { return items.slice(start, size); }

evidence_items.output_snippet: Call `page` with a positive `start` while `size` represents the requested page length, as established by the previous implementation.

assumptions: The established contract treats `size` as the number of requested items, as indicated by the removed implementation and the function name.
limitations: Only the supplied one-line diff was reviewed; callers, tests, and additional input validation were not provided.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore the exclusive end calculation: `items.slice(start, start + size)`.

finding.title: Preserve a valid zero timeout
finding.explanation: Replacing nullish coalescing with logical OR changes the function's contract for falsy numbers. In particular, `timeout(0)` previously returned `0` but now returns `30`. The declared input type permits zero, and no supplied guard establishes that it is invalid.
finding.user_impact: Callers using zero for immediate expiration or to disable waiting will silently receive a 30-unit timeout instead.

evidence_items.output_snippet: Call `timeout(0)`. The change also defaults `NaN`, although whether that input is supported is not established by the supplied context.

assumptions: Zero is valid because it is included by the declared `number | undefined` type and no contrary contract was supplied.
limitations: The supplied diff contains no callers or documentation, so the application-specific meaning and unit of the timeout cannot be established.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore `value ?? 30`. If zero is intentionally invalid, reject or normalize it explicitly and document the revised API contract.

finding.title: Iterating the mapping directly makes pruning fail on deletions
finding.explanation: The previous `list(values)` created a stable key snapshot. The new loop iterates the live mapping while deleting entries from it. For a normal Python `dict`, deleting the first key whose value is `None` changes the dictionary size, and advancing the iterator then raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. The function may therefore leave the input only partially pruned before failing. The issue is avoided only when no entry is deleted.
finding.user_impact: Callers passing a dictionary containing at least one `None` value can receive an unexpected runtime exception and observe a partially modified dictionary.

evidence_items.output_snippet: `values` is a standard Python dictionary with one or more entries whose value is `None`.

assumptions: `values` is intended to support normal dictionary semantics, as implied by key lookup and deletion.
limitations: No callers or tests were supplied, so the handling expected for non-dictionary custom mappings cannot be established.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore iteration over a snapshot, such as `for key in list(values):`, before deleting keys.

finding.title: Return the task promise instead of detaching it
finding.explanation: Previously, `save` returned the task's result, allowing callers to observe completion and failure. The new implementation discards that result and suppresses every rejection. A caller that does `await save(task)` will now continue immediately because `save` returns `undefined`, and it cannot learn that the save failed.
finding.user_impact: Callers may report success or proceed with dependent work before the task completes, while task failures become silent.

evidence_items.output_snippet: An asynchronous task is passed and a caller relies on the returned promise for sequencing or error handling, especially when the task rejects.

assumptions: The prior return value is part of the callable API; no affected callers were supplied to confirm otherwise.
limitations: The supplied diff does not establish whether fire-and-forget behavior was intentional.
finding.proposed_remedy: Return the task promise, preferably `return task();`, so callers retain completion and rejection handling. If rejection must be handled here, return the chained promise and perform meaningful handling rather than using an empty catch.

finding.title: Preserve support for synchronous task results
finding.explanation: The previous implementation accepted a task returning any value. Calling `.catch` unconditionally now requires the result to be a Promise-like object, causing an otherwise successful synchronous task to throw a `TypeError`.
finding.user_impact: Existing synchronous task callbacks can fail after performing their work, changing successful calls into exceptions.

evidence_items.output_snippet: `task()` returns a non-thenable value such as `undefined`, a boolean, or an object.

assumptions: The function's prior acceptance of arbitrary task return values was intentional compatibility behavior.
limitations: No type declarations or callers were supplied to show whether `task` is contractually required to return a Promise.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore `return task();`. If uniform promise handling is required, use `return Promise.resolve().then(task)` and preserve the returned promise for callers.

finding.title: Binary floating-point truncation can undercount cents
finding.explanation: The changed expression performs multiplication using the input's native arithmetic before truncating with `int`. For float inputs, binary representation can produce a value just below the intended whole number; for example, `0.29 * 100` is approximately `28.999999999999996`, so this implementation returns `28`. The previous conversion through `Decimal(str(value))` returns `29` for that input.
finding.user_impact: Amounts represented as floats can be understated by one cent, affecting prices, balances, or totals.

evidence_items.output_snippet: Call `cents` with a float whose multiplication by 100 lies just below the intended integer due to binary floating-point representation, such as `0.29`.

assumptions: `cents` is intended to convert ordinary decimal monetary values to their corresponding integer cent amount.
Truncation of fractional cents was intentional in the previous implementation; the supplied context does not establish a different rounding policy.
limitations: No callers or tests were supplied, so the concrete input types used by the project cannot be confirmed.
finding.proposed_remedy: Retain decimal arithmetic, such as `int(Decimal(str(value)) * 100)`, with the `Decimal` import restored. If fractional cents require a particular rounding policy, apply an explicit `Decimal.quantize` rule before conversion.

finding.title: Numeric string inputs no longer work
finding.explanation: The previous implementation normalized the input with `str(value)` and passed it to `Decimal`, so values such as `'1.23'` were accepted. The new expression applies Python's string repetition semantics first: `'1.23' * 100` produces a repeated dotted string, which `int(...)` rejects with `ValueError`.
finding.user_impact: Existing callers that pass amounts from forms, JSON-adjacent data, configuration, or other text sources can now fail instead of receiving a cent value.

evidence_items.output_snippet: Call `cents` with a valid decimal amount encoded as a string, such as `'1.23'`.

assumptions: Accepting numeric strings was part of the effective API because the previous implementation handled them explicitly.
No supplied context shows an intentional decision to narrow the accepted input types.
limitations: The function's declared API and callers were not supplied, so it is unresolved whether string inputs are relied upon in this repository.
finding.proposed_remedy: Restore conversion through `Decimal(str(value))`, or explicitly parse and validate accepted string inputs before multiplying. If strings are intentionally unsupported, enforce and document the narrowed input contract and update all affected callers.
